source.title: Contrastive Weak-to-strong Generalization
source.authors: Hou-Cheng Jiang; Jun-Feng Fang; Jia-Xing Wu; Tian-Yu Zhang; Chen Gao; Yong Li; Xiang Wang; Xiang-Nan He; Yang Deng

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests weak-to-strong training and compares a new contrastive-labeling method with weak-supervision baselines, but does not calculate Burns et al.'s PGR measure.
record.gate_note: The paper reports average benchmark scores (an explicitly reported average across benchmarks) for weak-to-strong methods and models, plus text-described and figure-only effects of model scale and contrastive coefficient. It does not calculate PGR or report a strong model trained on true labels as a ceiling. Reward and response-length analyses in Figure 2 are about generated samples, not the trained student's performance, so they are not recorded as outcome rows.
record.test_reason: Strong instruct models (7B/8B) are trained on samples from aligned 3B weak models and compared with the weak supervisor and with weak-to-strong baselines (naive Weak SFT, AuxConf). The task is generative preference alignment, scored by AlpacaEval2/Arena-Hard averages. No strong ceiling is reported and PGR is not computed, but whether the student beats the supervisor can be read directly.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also claim that the other weak-to-strong baselines (Weak SFT, AuxConf, WSPO) can degrade the strong model below its base, while ConG preserves downstream capabilities. They state that gains grow with larger strong models and smaller capability gaps.
record.recipe_differences: Uses contrastive decoding between pre- and post-alignment weak models to create SFT samples, followed by DPO using those samples paired with strong-model generations; the paper compares this with Weak SFT, AuxConf and other baselines rather than reproducing Burns et al.'s recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment results vary with the contrastive coefficient α and weak–strong model capability gap. Cross-family results are described as slightly lower than in-family results. Evaluation scores are also reported under different judges, with relative ordering stated to remain unchanged.

fits_no_version.finding: Contrastive-decoding samples from the weak models have higher implicit reward. Explicit reward stays high for α≤0.5 and drops sharply above it (Figure 2). This is about the quality of the supervision data, not student performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Quality of weak-supervisor samples (implicit/explicit reward) as a predictor of weak-to-strong gains.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: PGR is not calculated, and no strong true-label ceiling is reported. The main tables' Avg. entries have no separately stated uncertainty. Some model-gap and α results are described in text but their individual plotted values are not stated. The human evaluation uses 10% of the evaluation, and the paper gives no uncertainty for those averages.
record.rows_left_out: Individual LC, SC and WR components were not separately extracted where the reported Avg. row and accompanying text capture the claim-relevant result; the paper reports those components in Tables 1, 3, 5 and 6. Figure-only numerical values for the model-gap and α sweeps were not transcribed; their text-described findings are recorded in r11, r12 and r19.

untested.parts: No strong model trained on ground-truth preferences, so PGR cannot be computed.
Ensembling weak supervisors; loss variants other than AuxConf.
Chess, reward modelling, classification tasks; predictors from representations; PGR as the measure.
Entire version: exploitation of supervisor blind spots, distribution shift, shared errors.
Entire version: theory is about contrastive decoding and implicit reward, not student-beats-supervisor conditions.

missing.what: WeakTeacher and WSPO students vs the weak supervisor. WeakTeacher 43.5 > 37.8 (Qwen) but 32.6 < 33.5 (Llama); WSPO 25.6 and 18.1, both below the supervisor.
Weak SFT (pre) students: 23.4 and 14.1, far below both the supervisor and the strong base.
Weak models self-aligned with ConG-S/ConG (42.4/45.5 Qwen-3B; 32.2/34.6 Llama-3B). These are the closer supervisor comparators for the ConG students.
General-capability cost. Weak SFT and AuxConf drop the strong models by up to about 5.6 points on ARC, MMLU and GSM8K; ConG/ConG-S stay within about 1.3 points.
Per-transition numeric values for the capability-gap and α sweeps.

record.verdict_notes: The setting is generative preference alignment judged by LLM win rates, not Burns' classification PGR. The weak supervisor was DPO-aligned using ArmoRM reward-model rankings. Text–table inconsistencies: cross-family ConG is reported as 42.1 in the text but 42.8 in Table 3, and the 'slightly lower than in-family' claim contradicts the Qwen→Llama numbers. The human evaluation covers only 10% of items and gives no uncertainty.

versions.untested_parts: The paper compares trained students with weak-model results, but does not calculate PGR or provide a strong model trained on true labels as the ceiling.
Tests contrastive decoding with SFT and DPO against weak-SFT and other baselines, including AuxConf; does not test ensembling weak supervisors or a range of loss variants.
Tests model transitions, cross-family transfer and instruction-following benchmarks. Does not test chess, reward modelling, or predictors based on internal representations.
Does not test exploitation of supervisor blind spots, distribution shift, or shared weak/strong errors.
The theoretical analysis concerns contrastive decoding and implicit rewards, not conditions under which a student must beat its supervisor.
No vision or other non-language modality is tested.
